newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil to hold final sugar plan talks on Thursday.
newsitem.headline: Brazil to hold final sugar plan talks on Thursday.

text.p: Representatives from Brazil's private sugar sector and government officials are to hold hopefully a final meeting on the 1997/98 sugar crop plan on April 24, said a top government sugar official.
"For me, this will be the decisive meeting," said Pedro Cabral, head of the sugar and alcohol department at the Industry and Commerce Ministry.

The crop plan should be published on April 30 ahead of the traditional May 1 start of the center-south harvest but talks have been dogged by a battle between the Industry and Commerce Ministry and Sao Paulo state, the country's largest producer.
Previously the crop plan has detailed production of sugar and alcohol as well as export allowances per factory.

But while Sao Paulo producers accept there should be a plan for alcohol and for the internal sugar market, they do not want to see a set figure for exports but would rather producers be allowed to sell abroad whatever was not needed elsewhere.
"We do not accept export quotas," said a spokesman for the Sao Paulo Alcohol and Industry Association.
In order to apply political pressure, the state has not submited a proposed breakdown for exports per factory and does not intend to do so at tomorrow's meeting, the spokesman said.
This however will not delay the publication of the crop plan, Cabral said.
"Who decides on the crop plan is the Industry and Commerce Ministry. The crop plan will be published on April 30," he said.
"If they do not submit the figures, we will try and calculate them," he added.

The government has already said its priority this year is to produce enough alcohol to eliminate the need for imports and despite expectations of a higher cane crop, sugar production will only be marginally higher than last year, Cabral said.
"Sugar cane production should be higher so sugar output should rise a little, but only a very little," Cabral said.
Brazilian sugar output was around 13.5 million tonnes in 1996/97 including 10.43 million tonnes from the center-south.

Center-south cane production is expected to grow between five and eight percent on 1996/97 levels of 231.60 million tonnes and already some factories have begun crushing in the second half of April, the AIAA spokesman said.

But the total amount of sugar available for export from Brazil in 1997/98 is not expected to be greatly higher than in 1996/97 when 5.2 million tonnes were earmarked in the crop plan for the overseas market.

Last year the government initially authorised only 80 percent of this total free of export tax in order to be able to monitor internal market supply but this year the full export quota would be released from the outset, Cabral said.
